newsitem.title: THAILAND: Clinton visit to Thailand to help boost trade.
newsitem.headline: Clinton visit to Thailand to help boost trade.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton's brief visit to Bangkok this week is seen as an opportunity for him to show America's interest in Asia and help boost trade in Thailand, Thai and U.S. diplomats said.
Clinton is due to arrive in Bangkok late on Monday night for a 27-hour stay -- the first presidential visit to Thailand in 27 years.

"The basic purpose for this state visit, which is to honour the 50th anniversary of His Majesty King Bhumibol (Adulyadej's) accession to the throne, is just to renew an old friendship and visit an ally in the region," a U.S. diplomat said.

Clinton's trip to Bangkok is the last leg of his first overseas trip since being re-elected earlier this month. The 12-day tour took him on a working holiday to Australia, then to the Philippines for meetings of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.
Thai diplomats say a presidential visit -- the last was in 1969 by Richard Nixon during the Vietnam War -- is a good opportunity to boost commercial ties.
"It shows the importance the U.S. attaches to Thailand, and this country's importance in Southeast Asia," Nitya Pibulsonggram, Thailand's ambassador to Washington, said.

Although Thailand's economy has slowed this year, it was cited by the World Bank as the fastest-growing economy in the world during the past decade and was a good opportunity for American companies, a U.S. official said.
Two-way trade amounts to about $18 billion, and Thai exports to the United States -- its biggest single export market -- outweighed imports by several billion dollars in 1995.
Economic analysts hope a tax treaty to be signed by Clinton and Thai officials during the visit will help boost trade.

The treaty, which took more than a decade of negotiations to hammer out, removes double taxation of earnings with the goal of encouraging more investment and technology transfer between the U.S. and Thailand.
Clinton is due to discuss economic and security issues with the Thai premier as well as the drug trade and trafficking still rampant in the region.
But since Thailand is in the throes of a government transition, the question of who Clinton will meet as prime minister is still to be determined.

Clinton's visit may hasten proceedings to enable New Aspiration Party (NAP) leader Chavalit Yongchaiyudh to be sworn in as prime minister, replacing Chart Thai caretaker premier Banharn Silpa-archa, by Monday.
Chavalit's NAP won a slim victory in a November 17 general election. Normally it would take about two weeks for a premier to be sworn in.

Clinton is due to give a speech at Bangkok's Chulalongkorn University on Tuesday afternoon. He and his wife, Hillary Clinton, on a separate visit to northern Thailand on Sunday and Monday, will leave for the U.S. about midnight on Tuesday.
